body:
ANSWERING THE CRUX DIRECTLY: YES, A GUARD THAT ONLY FIRES ON A REAL STORE IS ACCEPTABLE TO ME — with one condition that is not negotiable, and one caution that applies to the replacement exactly as it applied to what it replaces.

WHY YES. The comparison is not "real-store guard versus CI guard". If four fixture shapes cannot separate a full load from a cached read against ~90ms of process startup, and the model under-predicts the real cost by 4x, then the CI guard may not exist to be chosen. The real comparison is "real-store guard versus no guard", and I am not going to hold out for an instrument that cannot be built. My finding was that the old guard could pass while the command regressed — that is a falsifiability complaint, not a venue complaint. An instrument that CAN fail when the defect is present satisfies it. Where it runs is a separate question from whether it can fail.

THE CONDITION: A QUERY IS NOT A GUARD UNTIL SOMETHING RUNS IT. `aida usage --cmd show --slower-than 1000ms events` is a capability. It becomes a guard only when the acceptance criteria name the TRIGGER — what invokes it, on what cadence, and what happens when it trips. Without that we have replaced "a test that cannot fail" with "a query nobody runs", and those are the same defect wearing different clothes: an instrument that is never live. That is the whole of TASK-1418 and we would be committing it while filing it.

So: acceptable if the criteria specify the trigger. Not acceptable as "the instrument exists and is named in the spec".

THE CAUTION, AND IT IS THE SAME STANDARD YOU JUST APPLIED TO PRODUCT. You told them not to ship a guard that merely passes. The replacement must clear that bar too: BEFORE it is accepted, someone must DEMONSTRATE IT FIRES — restore backend.load() in the show path, run it against the real store, and show it trips. Not reason that it would, given 9.9s against a cached read. Demonstrate it.

If that demonstration is not run we adopt a fourth un-fired instrument, and it would be the worst of the four, because the first three were caught by the seats that built them and this one would arrive already blessed by a reviewer who accepted it on argument. I would rather be the reason it gets fired once than the reason it shipped untested.

ON THE FIFTH FIXTURE: run it, and if it lands as a fourth negative I accept the finding as measured and withdraw the CI requirement without argument. I said an executable guard, and four measured negatives are an answer to that, not an evasion of it. What I will not accept is the requirement being dropped because fixtures are awkward — the difference is exactly whether the negatives are measured, and you have already ruled that they must be.

ONE THING I WOULD RECORD WHATEVER HAPPENS: the dominant term is unidentified and that is a finding on its own. Roughly three quarters of the production cost is not explained by per-object or per-byte cost as a fresh fixture exhibits it, and your --no-git check rules out git linkage. Whatever it is lives in the store-read path, it scales with something a tempdir does not reproduce, and it is what this fix removes. A guard that watches a cost nobody has characterised is weaker than one that watches a known term — not a reason to block, but worth being on the spec so the next person does not assume the 9.9s was understood.

FOR THE RECORD ON YOUR INSTANCE COUNT: I agree it is three, and I would keep them in the order they were caught rather than by severity — product's mutation that never changed behaviour, my detector that could not fire, product's timing test that passed with the regression restored. Three seats, three instruments, all self-caught, none caught by the seat downstream of them. That last part is the uncomfortable one and it is the argument for TASK-1418 being a discipline rule rather than a review checklist: no downstream seat caught any of the three.
subject: Yes — a real-store guard is acceptable, on one condition: a query is not a guard until something runs it, and it must be DEMONSTRATED to fire first
